```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(ddplot)
```

`D3.js` is a famous JavaScript library that allows one to create extremely flexible SVG graphics however `D3` has (at least according to me) a pretty steep learning curve. Further, in order to understand some core concepts, one need to have some basics in `HTML`, `CSS` and `JavaScript`. `ddplot` aims to simply the process using a set of functions that render several graphics using a simple `R` API. Finally, `ddplot` is built upon the amazing `r2d3` package which makes it a breeze to interface `D3.js` with `R`, so a big thanks to the developers.

# `scatter_plot()`

Let's work with the `mpg` data frame from the `ggplot2` package.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2) # needed for the mpg data frame

scatter_plot(
  data = mpg,
  x = "hwy",
  y = "cty",
  xtitle = "hwy variable",
  ytitle = "cty variable",
  title = "cty and hwy relationship",
  titleFontSize = 20
)

```

In comparison to `ggplot2`, graphics' customization in `ddplot` is limited nonetheless you get a fully vectorized SVG which is cool.



```{r, fig.align='center'}
scatter_plot(
  data = mpg,
  x = "displ",
  y = "cty",
  col = "tomato",
  bgcol = "pink",
  size = 3,
  stroke = "royalblue",
  strokeWidth = 1,
  xtitle = "displ variable",
  ytitle = "cty variable",
  xticks = 3,
  yticks = 3)

```

# `histogram()`

The `histogram()` function allows you to visualize the distribution of a vector of data:

```{r}
histogram(
  x = mpg$hwy,
  bins = 20,
  fill = "crimson",
  stroke = "white",
  strokeWidth = 1,
  title = "Distribution of the hwy variable",
  width = "20",
  height = "10"
)
```


# `animated_histogram()`

This function allows you to create a one-click histogram animation. Useful for presentation purposes. Click on the following empty plot and see what happens:

```{r}
animated_histogram(
  x = mpg$hwy,
  duration = 2000,
  delay = 100,
  fill = "lime",
  stroke = "white",
  bgcol = "white"
  )
```

Note that you can customize the animation using the two parameters `duration` and `delay`.


# `flower()` 

The `flower()` function allows you to plot a simple flowers with a defined number of petals. You can also define the width/length of the petals and rotate them if needed: 


```{r}
flower(
  petalCount = 7,
  petalColor = "plum",
  rotationSpeed = 0
)
```


```{r}
flower(
  petalCount = 15,
  petalWidth = 20,
  petalColor = "plum",
  rotationSpeed = 1.5
)
```


# `heart_fill`

The `heart_fill` function allows you to display a heart indicator which will be filled according to a numerical value from 0 to 1: 

```{r}
heart_fill(fill_level = 0.8, titleText = NULL, renderFillLabel = FALSE)
```

# `glass_fill` 

The `glass_fill` function works the same way as the `heart_fill` above: 

```{r}
glass_fill(fill_level = 0.8, titleText = "Glass of water", renderFillLabel = TRUE)
```

# `plant_growth`

The `plant_growth` function can also be used as a visual clue: 

```{r}
plant_growth(0.4)
```
```{r}
plant_growth(1)
```


# `pulse_grid()`

The `pulse_grid()` function is useful when you have a compact matrix of values and you want the viewer to immediately spot where activity, load, risk, or pressure is concentrated. It works especially well for operational monitoring and staffing views because the pulsing highlights the hottest cells without requiring interaction.

## Example 1: Team workload by hour

This is a good fit for support teams, call centers, or editorial desks. Instead of reading a table of numbers, you can see which teams are under the heaviest load at which times of day.

```{r}
workload_grid <- data.frame(
  hour = c("09:00","12:00","15:00","18:00",
           "09:00","12:00","15:00","18:00",
           "09:00","12:00","15:00","18:00"),
  team = c("North","North","North","North",
           "South","South","South","South",
           "East","East","East","East"),
  load = c(0.35,0.72,0.56,0.91,
           0.41,0.67,0.83,0.58,
           0.28,0.49,0.77,0.63),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

pulse_grid(
  data = workload_grid,
  x = "hour",
  y = "team",
  value = "load",
  title = "Support Team Load Through the Day",
  low = "#D9F0FF",
  high = "red",
  bgcol = "#0B132B",
  stroke = "#1C2541",
  strokeWidth = 1.5,
  pulseStrength = 0.22
)
```

Why this is useful: it gives managers a compact way to decide when to reallocate staff, stagger breaks, or add temporary coverage. The pulse effect makes the high-pressure windows stand out much faster than a plain heatmap.

## Example 2: Reliability monitoring by service and weekday

This second example works well for engineering or product teams. A pulse grid can summarize incident rate, latency, or error volume across services and days of the week, making it easier to see repeated pressure points in a weekly operating rhythm.

```{r}
reliability_grid <- data.frame(
  day = c(
    "Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri",
    "Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri",
    "Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri",
    "Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri"
  ),
  service = c(
    "API","API","API","API","API",
    "Billing","Billing","Billing","Billing","Billing",
    "Search","Search","Search","Search","Search",
    "Auth","Auth","Auth","Auth","Auth"
  ),
  incident_score = c(
    0.62, 0.44, 0.57, 0.78, 0.69,
    0.31, 0.36, 0.40, 0.51, 0.47,
    0.73, 0.81, 0.76, 0.88, 0.67,
    0.22, 0.27, 0.25, 0.34, 0.29
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

pulse_grid(
  data = reliability_grid,
  x = "day",
  y = "service",
  value = "incident_score",
  title = "Service Reliability Pressure Map",
  low = "lightgreen",
  high = "#B00020",
  bgcol = "#081C15",
  labelColor = "#F1FAEE",
  titleColor = "#F1FAEE",
  stroke = "#2D6A4F",
  showValues = TRUE,
  digits = 2
)
```

Why this is useful: repeated hot cells reveal where engineering effort should go first. In this example, a team can immediately see whether one service is consistently unstable or whether problems cluster around a particular day in the deployment cycle.


# `flame` 

You can create cool `flames` using the `flame` function, useful if you want to display the state of a critical information that yields a numerical values (for example, the number of errors encountered in a specific process):


```{r}
flame(
  intensity = 20, 
  flameGradientColors = c("yellow", "orange", "darkred"),
  flameOutline = "darkred",
  bgcol = "#fefefe"
)
```


```{r}
flame(
  intensity = 80, 
  flameGradientColors = c("green", "darkgreen", "darkblue"),
  flameOutline = "#fefefe",
  bgcol = "black"
)
```
# `parliament_chart()`

You can easily create a `Parliamant chart` using the `parliamant_chart()` function, consider the following example: 

```{r}
# The data is a toy example and does not reflect the reality
vote_results_germany <- data.frame(
    political_party = c("SDP", "CDU", "Linke", "Grüne"),
    number_of_seats = c(200, 40, 30, 20)
)
parliament_chart(
  data = vote_results_germany,
  categorical_column = "political_party",
  numerical_column = "number_of_seats",
  title = "German Bundestag",
  seatSize = 10,
  bgcol = "#fefefe"
)
```




# `bar_chart()`

The `barChat()` function allows you to create bar charts however you need to make the aggregation beforehand. In the following example, we will plot the average `cty` for each `manufacturer` using the `dplyr` package.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

mpg %>% group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%
  bar_chart(
    x = "manufacturer",
    y = "mean_cty",
    xFontSize = 10,
    yFontSize = 10,
    fill = "orange",
    strokeWidth = 2,
    ytitle = "average cty value",
    title = "Average City Miles per Gallon by manufacturer"
  )
```

The bars can be easily sorted in `ascending` or `descending` order using the `sort` parameter:


```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
mpg %>% group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%
  bar_chart(
    x = "manufacturer",
    y = "mean_cty",
    sort = "ascending",
    xFontSize = 10,
    yFontSize = 10,
    fill = "orange",
    strokeWidth = 1,
    ytitle = "average cty value",
    title = "Average City Miles per Gallon by manufacturer",
    titleFontSize = 16
  )
```


# `horz_bar_chart()`

If you've many categories, it might be a good idea to go for a horizontal bar chart. It has the same parameters as the `bar_chart()` function except that the x-axis parameter is named `value` and the y-axis parameter named `label`, this naming convention aims to mitigate some confusion that can arise.

If we want to replicate the above graphic in a horizontal way, we can do:

```{r}
mpg %>% group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%
  horz_bar_chart(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "mean_cty",
    sort = "ascending",
    labelFontSize  = 10,
    valueFontSize = 10,
    fill = "orange",
    stroke = "crimson",
    strokeWidth = 1,
    valueTitle  = "average cty value",
    title = "Average City Miles per Gallon by manufacturer",
    titleFontSize = 16
  )
```

As in `bar_chart()`, we can aslo sort in descending order:


```{r}
mpg %>% group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(mean_cty = mean(cty)) %>%
  horz_bar_chart(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "mean_cty",
    sort = "descending",
    labelFontSize  = 10,
    valueFontSize = 10,
    bgcol = "black",
    axisCol = "white",
    fill = "white",
    stroke = "white",
    strokeWidth = 1,
    valueTitle  = "average cty value",
    labelTitle = "Manufacturers",
    title = "Average City Miles per Gallon by manufacturer",
    titleFontSize = 16
  )
```


# `lollipop_chart()`

lollipop chart follows the same behavior as bar charts but instead of bars you get lollipops, hence the name. Below an example of a lollipop chart with `ddplot`:


```{r}
mpg %>% group_by(drv) %>%
  summarise(median_cty = median(cty)) %>%
  lollipop_chart(
    x = "drv",
    y = "median_cty",
    sort = "ascending",
    xtitle = "drv variable",
    ytitle = "median cty",
    title = "Median cty per drv",
    xFontSize = 20
  )
```


It's possible to grasp the distribution of some variable according to a specific categorical variable using the same function:


```{r}

mpg %>% filter(year == 2008) %>%
lollipop_chart(
    x = "manufacturer",
    y = "hwy",
    circleFill = 'red',
    circleStroke = 'orange',
    circleRadius = 5,
    sort = "none",
    xFontSize = 10
  )
```

From above, it's quite easy to notice that although Toyota has two cars with high highway miles per galon (hwy), it also produces many other vehicles with poor hwy.


# `horz_lollipop()`

Same with bar charts, if you have a variable that has many categorical values, you can work with the reversed version of `lollipop_chart()` which is `horz_lollipop()`:


```{r}
mpg %>% group_by(manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(median_cty = median(cty)) %>%
  horz_lollipop(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "median_cty",
    sort = "descending")
```
You can also do:



```{r}
mpg %>% filter(year == 2008) %>%
horz_lollipop(
    label = "manufacturer",
    value = "hwy",
    circleFill = 'red',
    circleStroke = 'orange',
    circleRadius = 5,
    sort = "none"
  )
```


# `pie_chart()`

Pie charts and donut charts are pretty straightforward to set up. We'll use a sample from the `starwars` data frame to plot a simple pie chart.


```{r}
# starwars is part of the dplyr data frame
mini_starwars <- starwars %>% tidyr::drop_na(mass) %>%
  sample_n(size = 5) # getting 5 random values

pie_chart(
  data = mini_starwars,
  value = "mass",
  label = "name"
)
```

Using the `padRadius`, `padAngle` and `cornerRadius` parameters, one can get fanciers pie charts:

```{r}
pie_chart(
  data = mini_starwars,
  value = "mass",
  label = "name",
  padRadius = 200,
  padAngle = 0.1,
  cornerRadius = 50,
  innerRadius = 10
)
```
If you need a donut chart, you just need to play with the `innerRadius` parameter:

```{r}
pie_chart(
  data = mini_starwars,
  value = "mass",
  label = "name",
  innerRadius = 120,
  cornerRadius = 20,
  title = "5 Starwars characters ranked by their mass",
  titleFontSize = 16,
  bgcol = "yellow"
)
```

# `line_chart()`

The `line_chart()` function is used to plot time series data. The use must provide a `date` variable that has the `yyyy-mm-dd` format. In the following example, we'll use the `Air Passenger` built-in `ts` data and convert it to a classical data frame:


```{r}
# 1. converting AirPassengers to a tidy data frame
airpassengers <- data.frame(
  passengers = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  date= zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

# 2. plotting the line chart
line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers"
)
```

You can modify the line interpolation using the `curve` parameter:

```{r}
line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  curve = "curveStep"
)
```


```{r}
line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  curve = "curveCardinal"
)
```

```{r}
line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  curve = "curveBasis"
)
```

# `anim_line_chart()`

Heavily inspired from [Jure Stabuc's example](https://observablehq.com/@jurestabuc/animated-line-chart), the `anim_line_chart()` function create an empty SVG but when each time you click on it a line chart animation starts. Note that the line lasts after the end of the animation. Go ahead, click on the empty graphic below:

```{r}
anim_line_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  duration = 10000, # in milliseconds (10 seconds)
  curve = "curveCardinal"
  )
```


# `area_chart()`

`area_chart()` works similarly except that instead of a line you get an area.


```{r}
# 1. converting AirPassengers to a tidy data frame
airpassengers <- data.frame(
  passengers = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  date= zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

# 2. plotting the area chart
area_chart(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  y = "passengers",
  fill = "purple",
  bgcol = "white"
)
```

# `area_band()`

`area_band()` lets you plot a filled area between two y-values. For the sake of the example, let's create an additional column `passengers_upper` that has an additional 40 passengers for each observation:

```{r}
airpassengers <- data.frame(
  passengers_lower = as.matrix(AirPassengers),
  passengers_upper = as.matrix(AirPassengers) + 40,
  date= zoo::as.Date(time(AirPassengers))
)

area_band(
  data = airpassengers,
  x = "date",
  yLower = "passengers_lower",
  yUpper = "passengers_upper",
  fill = "yellow",
  stroke = "black"
)
```


# `stacked_area_chart()`

This function allows you to create a stacked area chart. You need two components:

- A data frame in wide format (see an example below). If it's in wide format, you can still use `pivot_wider()` from the `tidyr` package to make wider.
- A date variable in `yyyy-mm-dd` format that will plotted in the x-axis.

Let's work with the following data frame (shortened) provided by [Mike Bostock in his stacked area chart example](https://observablehq.com/@d3/stacked-area-chart):

```{r}
data <- data.frame(
  date = c(
    "2000-01-01", "2000-02-01", "2000-03-01", "2000-04-01",
    "2000-05-01", "2000-06-01", "2000-07-01",
    "2000-08-01", "2000-09-01", "2000-10-01"
  ),
  Trade = c(
    2000,1023, 983, 2793, 1821, 1837, 1792, 1853, 791, 739
  ),
  Manufacturing = c(
    734, 694, 739, 736, 685, 621, 708, 685, 667, 693
  ),
  Leisure = c(
    1782, 1779, 1789, 658, 675, 833, 786, 675, 636, 691
  ),
  Agriculture = c(
    655, 587,623, 517, 561, 2545, 636, 584, 559, 2504
  )
)

data
```


Note that when running `stacked_area_chart()` all the variables available within the considered data frame will be plotted. If you want to restrict the plotting to only specific variables, just drop the unneeded columns:


```{r}
stacked_area_chart(
  data = data,
  x = "date",
  legendTextSize = 14
  )
```

You can modify the color scheme using the `colorCategory` parameter:


```{r}
stacked_area_chart(
  data = data,
  x = "date",
  legendTextSize = 14,
  curve = "curveCardinal",
  colorCategory = "Accent",
  bgcol = "white",
  stroke = "black",
  strokeWidth = 1
  )
```


```{r}
stacked_area_chart(
  data = data,
  x = "date",
  legendTextSize = 14,
  curve = "curveBasis",
  colorCategory = "Set3",
  bgcol = "black",
  axisCol = "white",
  xticks = 4,
  stroke = "black"
  )
```

You can find list of D3 categorical color schemes [here](https://github.com/d3/d3-scale-chromatic#categorical)

Finally, if you hover over the chart you'll notice a tooltip that identified the different area categories.

# `bar_chart_race()`

This function allows you to create an animated bar chart race. `bar_chart_race()` is similar to `bar_chart()` but takes a third variable mapped to the time dimension, with options for styling transitions.

Let's make a bar chart race of population growth among various countries using a subset of the `gapminder` dataset from the [{gapminder} package](https://github.com/jennybc/gapminder):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gapminder_subset <- gapminder::gapminder %>%
  select(country, year, pop) %>% 
  filter(country %in% c("Japan", "Mexico", "Germany", "Brazil", "Philippines", "Vietnam")) %>%
  mutate(pop = pop/1e6)


gapminder_subset %>%
  slice_sample(n = 10)

#>    year       pop     country
#> 1  2007  91.07729 Philippines
#> 2  1997  76.04900     Vietnam
#> 3  1972 107.18827       Japan
#> 4  1967  39.46391     Vietnam
#> 5  1952  30.14432      Mexico
#> 6  1987 142.93808      Brazil
#> 7  1997 168.54672      Brazil
#> 8  1962  41.12148      Mexico
#> 9  1952  69.14595     Germany
#> 10 1957  91.56301       Japan
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}
gapminder_subset <- data.frame(
  year = c(
    1952L,1957L,1962L,1967L,1972L,1977L,
    1982L,1987L,1992L,1997L,2002L,2007L,1952L,1957L,1962L,
    1967L,1972L,1977L,1982L,1987L,1992L,1997L,2002L,2007L,
    1952L,1957L,1962L,1967L,1972L,1977L,1982L,1987L,1992L,
    1997L,2002L,2007L,1952L,1957L,1962L,1967L,1972L,1977L,
    1982L,1987L,1992L,1997L,2002L,2007L,1952L,1957L,1962L,
    1967L,1972L,1977L,1982L,1987L,1992L,1997L,2002L,2007L,
    1952L,1957L,1962L,1967L,1972L,1977L,1982L,1987L,1992L,
    1997L,2002L,2007L
  ),
  pop = c(
    56.60256,65.551171,76.03939,88.049823,
    100.840058,114.313951,128.962939,142.938076,155.975974,
    168.546719,179.914212,190.010647,69.145952,71.019069,73.739117,
    76.368453,78.717088,78.160773,78.335266,77.718298,
    80.597764,82.011073,82.350671,82.400996,86.459025,91.563009,
    95.831757,100.825279,107.188273,113.872473,118.454974,
    122.091325,124.329269,125.956499,127.065841,127.467972,30.144317,
    35.015548,41.121485,47.995559,55.984294,63.759976,
    71.640904,80.122492,88.11103,95.895146,102.479927,108.700891,
    22.438691,26.072194,30.325264,35.3566,40.850141,46.850962,
    53.456774,60.017788,67.185766,75.012988,82.995088,91.077287,
    26.246839,28.998543,33.79614,39.46391,44.655014,50.533506,
    56.142181,62.826491,69.940728,76.048996,80.908147,
    85.262356
  ),
  country = as.factor(c(
    "Brazil","Brazil",
    "Brazil","Brazil","Brazil","Brazil","Brazil",
    "Brazil","Brazil","Brazil","Brazil","Brazil","Germany",
    "Germany","Germany","Germany","Germany",
    "Germany","Germany","Germany","Germany","Germany",
    "Germany","Germany","Japan","Japan","Japan","Japan",
    "Japan","Japan","Japan","Japan","Japan","Japan",
    "Japan","Japan","Mexico","Mexico","Mexico",
    "Mexico","Mexico","Mexico","Mexico","Mexico",
    "Mexico","Mexico","Mexico","Mexico","Philippines",
    "Philippines","Philippines","Philippines","Philippines",
    "Philippines","Philippines","Philippines",
    "Philippines","Philippines","Philippines","Philippines",
    "Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam",
    "Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam",
    "Vietnam","Vietnam","Vietnam"
  ))
)
```

In this example, we simply pass call `bar_chart_race()` like `bar_chart()`, but with an additional variable mapped to the time dimension specified with `time = year`:

```{r}
gapminder_subset %>%
  bar_chart_race(
    x = "pop",
    y = "country",
    time = "year",
    ytitle = "Country",
    xtitle = "Population (in millions)",
    title = "Bar chart race of country populations"
  )
```

You can also stylize transitions with the `frameDur`, `transitionDur`,  and `ease` arguments. For example, setting the time spent pausing on each frame to zero with `frameDur = 0` will create a smooth animation:

```{r}
gapminder_subset %>%
  bar_chart_race(
    x = "pop",
    y = "country",
    time = "year",
    transitionDur = 1000,
    frameDur = 0,
    ytitle = "Country",
    xtitle = "Population (in millions)",
    title = "Bar chart race of country populations"
  )
```

As you might have noticed, the value of the column passed to the `time` argument is automatically labelled at the bottom-right corner of the plot panel. We can stylize this with a list of options passed to the `timeLabelOpts` argument (or turn it off with `timeLabel = FALSE`). We also give the bars a little bounce here with `ease = "BackInOut"` for fun.

```{r}
gapminder_subset %>%
  bar_chart_race(
    x = "pop",
    y = "country",
    time = "year",
    ease = "BackInOut",
    ytitle = "Country",
    xtitle = "Population (in millions)",
    title = "Bar chart race of country populations",
    timeLabelOpts = list(
      size = 40,
      prefix = "Year: ",
      xOffset = 0.2
    )
  )
```


# `liquid_chart()`

`liquid_chart()` renders a single value as a circle filled with an animated liquid. The water rises from empty to the target level on load, two staggered wave layers give the surface a natural depth, and the label text switches color at the water line — appearing in `textColor` above the surface and in `waveTextColor` inside the water.

```{r}
liquid_chart(value = 0.55, title = "Memory")
```

Colors, wave behaviour, and the label are all configurable:

```{r}
liquid_chart(
  value         = 0.28,
  label         = "28%",
  fillColor     = "tomato",
  circleColor   = "tomato",
  textColor     = "tomato",
  waveTextColor = "white",
  title         = "Errors"
)
```

```{r}
liquid_chart(
  value         = 0.72,
  label         = "72%",
  fillColor     = "#27ae60",
  waveAmplitude = 0.05,
  waveCount     = 3,
  waveSpeed     = 1.5,
  title         = "Battery"
)
```

# `waterfall_chart()`

A waterfall chart shows how an initial value is built up or eroded by a sequence of positive and negative contributions. Each bar starts exactly where the previous one ended. It is the standard chart for P&L decomposition, budget variance analysis, and any "what changed and why" narrative.

The optional `measure` column lets you mark certain bars as `"total"`, they span from zero to the running cumulative sum, making subtotals and final totals visually distinct. **Hovering over any bar shows a tooltip** with the label, the delta, and the running total.

```{r}
pnl <- data.frame(
  label   = c("Revenue", "COGS", "Gross Profit",
              "R&D", "S&M", "G&A", "Operating Income"),
  value   = c(1200, -450, 750, -120, -90, -60, 480),
  measure = c("relative", "relative", "total",
              "relative", "relative", "relative", "total")
)

waterfall_chart(
  data   = pnl,
  x      = "label",
  y      = "value",
  measure = "measure",
  title  = "P&L bridge",
  ytitle = "USD thousands"
)
```

Without a `measure` column every bar is a simple delta — useful for tracking a running balance over time:

```{r}
cashflow <- data.frame(
  month = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"),
  delta = c(120, -30, 80, -60, 95, -20)
)

waterfall_chart(
  data          = cashflow,
  x             = "month",
  y             = "delta",
  title         = "Monthly cash flow",
  ytitle        = "USD thousands",
  positiveColor = "steelblue",
  negativeColor = "tomato"
)
```

# `dumbbell_chart()`

A dumbbell chart (also called a connected dot plot) shows two values per category as dots joined by a horizontal line. It is the clearest way to communicate the gap or change between two groups, time points, or conditions across many categories , a grouped bar chart would require much more visual scanning to reach the same conclusion. The New York Times and The Economist use this format regularly.

```{r}
life_exp <- data.frame(
  country   = c("Brazil", "China", "Egypt", "India",
                "Japan", "Mexico", "Nigeria", "Turkey"),
  year_1952 = c(50.9, 44.0, 41.9, 37.4, 63.0, 50.8, 36.3, 43.6),
  year_2007 = c(72.4, 72.9, 71.3, 64.7, 82.6, 76.2, 46.9, 71.8)
)

dumbbell_chart(
  data     = life_exp,
  x1       = "year_1952",
  x2       = "year_2007",
  y        = "country",
  x1Label  = "1952",
  x2Label  = "2007",
  title    = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007",
  xtitle   = "Life expectancy (years)",
  sort     = "ascending"
)
```

The chart works equally well for comparing two conditions within the same time period. Here we compare average city and highway fuel economy across vehicle classes using the `mpg` dataset:

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

mpg_summary <- mpg |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(city = mean(cty), highway = mean(hwy))

dumbbell_chart(
  data    = mpg_summary,
  x1      = "city",
  x2      = "highway",
  y       = "class",
  x1Label = "City",
  x2Label = "Highway",
  col1    = "steelblue",
  col2    = "darkorange",
  title   = "City vs highway fuel economy by class",
  xtitle  = "Miles per gallon",
  sort    = "ascending"
)
```

# `beeswarm_plot()`

A beeswarm plot shows every individual data point along a numeric axis, spreading them sideways so they never overlap. It is far more transparent than a box plot because nothing is hidden behind a summary statistic — you see the full shape, outliers, and clusters of the raw data. The New York Times graphics desk uses this style regularly to remind readers that numbers represent real people.

The layout is computed with a D3 force simulation: each point is pulled toward its true value on the x-axis while a collision force prevents any two circles from touching.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset

# Single swarm — full distribution of highway fuel economy
beeswarm_plot(
  data   = mpg,
  x      = "hwy",
  col    = "steelblue",
  xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title  = "Distribution of hwy"
)
```

When a `group` column is provided, one swarm is drawn per group and colored automatically:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
beeswarm_plot(
  data   = mpg,
  x      = "hwy",
  group  = "class",
  xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title  = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class", 
  tooltip = "manufacturer"
)
```



You can swap the dataset and adjust the look freely. Here using the built-in `iris` dataset with a different color palette and larger points:

```{r fig.align='center'}
beeswarm_plot(
  data         = iris,
  x            = "Sepal.Length",
  group        = "Species",
  colorPalette = "Set2",
  radius       = 5,
  opacity      = 0.8,
  xtitle       = "Sepal length (cm)",
  title        = "Sepal length by species"
)
```

# `bullet_chart()`

The `bullet_chart()` function renders a bullet chart — a compact alternative to gauge charts designed by Stephen Few. It displays one actual value (the dark bar) against shaded qualitative bands (e.g. poor / satisfactory / good) and an optional target marker (the short vertical line).

The `ranges` argument defines the upper bound of each band; the first band starts at `min` (default 0). Colors default to a sequence of grays from darker (lower range) to lighter (higher range).

```{r}
bullet_chart(
  value    = 270,
  target   = 300,
  ranges   = c(150, 225, 350),
  title    = "Revenue",
  subtitle = "USD thousands"
)
```

You can stack several bullet charts side by side to compare multiple KPIs at a glance:

```{r}
bullet_chart(
  value      = 7.4,
  target     = 8.0,
  ranges     = c(4, 7, 10),
  title      = "Satisfaction",
  subtitle   = "out of 10",
  valueColor = "steelblue"
)
```

When a lower value is better (e.g. response time), simply order your `rangeColors` from lightest (best, lowest range) to darkest (worst, highest range):

```{r}
bullet_chart(
  value       = 320,
  target      = 250,
  ranges      = c(200, 500, 1000),
  rangeColors = c("#f0f0f0", "#d9d9d9", "#bdbdbd"),
  title       = "Response",
  subtitle    = "ms"
)
```

# `gauge_chart()` 

The `gauge_chart()` function renders a speedometer-style gauge. It takes a single numeric `value` and displays it on a circular dial spanning from `min` to `max`. The arc is divided into three zones: normal (plain), warning, and danger, each with its own color.

```{r}
gauge_chart(
  value = 8,
  title = "Memory"
)
```

You can adjust the thresholds and colors to match your context. Here the warning zone starts at 60% and the danger zone at 80%:

```{r}
gauge_chart(
  value = 72,
  min = 0,
  max = 100,
  title = "CPU Load",
  warningZone  = 60,
  warningColor = "orange",
  dangerZone   = 80,
  dangerColor  = "red"
)
```

The gauge is not limited to percentages, any numeric range works. Below is an example monitoring server response time in milliseconds, where anything above 400 ms is a warning and above 700 ms is critical:

```{r}
gauge_chart(
  value = 530,
  min = 0,
  max = 1000,
  title = "Response (ms)",
  warningZone  = 400,
  warningColor = "orange",
  dangerZone   = 700,
  dangerColor  = "red"
)
```

# `slope_chart()`

A slope chart (or slopegraph) places two values per category on two vertical axes, typically "before" and "after" or two different years, and connects them with a straight line. The steepness and direction of each line tell you at a glance who rose, who fell, and how the ranking changed. Edward Tufte popularised the form in *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (1983) with his chart of government receipts across rich countries, and the New York Times graphics desk has used it regularly ever since. Use it when you have a small-to-moderate number of categories measured at exactly two points; with many categories or many time points, a line chart is the better choice.

Each line is labelled with its category name and value at both ends, and labels that would overlap are nudged apart vertically. By default lines are colored by direction (increase or decrease). Hover over a line to emphasise it and fade the others.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Current receipts of government as a percentage of GDP, 1970 vs 1979
# (adapted from Edward Tufte's classic slopegraph)
receipts <- data.frame(
  country = c("Sweden", "Netherlands", "Norway", "Britain", "France",
              "Germany", "Belgium", "Canada", "Finland", "Italy",
              "United States", "Greece", "Switzerland", "Spain", "Japan"),
  y1970 = c(46.9, 44.0, 43.5, 40.7, 39.0, 37.5, 35.2, 35.2, 34.9, 30.4,
            30.3, 26.8, 26.5, 22.5, 20.7),
  y1979 = c(57.4, 55.8, 52.2, 39.0, 43.4, 42.9, 43.2, 35.8, 38.2, 35.7,
            32.5, 30.6, 33.2, 27.1, 26.6)
)

slope_chart(
  data       = receipts,
  start      = "y1970",
  end        = "y1979",
  group      = "country",
  startLabel = "1970",
  endLabel   = "1979",
  digits     = 1,
  title      = "Government receipts as % of GDP",
  height     = 520
)
```

Use `highlight` to tell a story about a few categories: the rest are drawn in a muted grey so they give context without competing for attention. Here we compare life expectancy in 1952 and 2007 using the `gapminder` dataset:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

countries <- c("China", "India", "Japan", "Brazil", "Nigeria",
               "Egypt", "Germany", "United States", "South Africa")

life <- filter(gapminder, year %in% c(1952, 2007), country %in% countries)
life <- select(life, country, year, lifeExp)
life <- pivot_wider(life, names_from = year, values_from = lifeExp,
                    names_prefix = "y")

slope_chart(
  data       = life,
  start      = "y1952",
  end        = "y2007",
  group      = "country",
  startLabel = "1952",
  endLabel   = "2007",
  highlight  = c("China", "South Africa"),
  digits     = 1,
  title      = "Life expectancy: 1952 vs 2007"
)
```

# `bump_chart()`

A bump chart shows how the *rank* of several entities changes from one period to the next. Each entity is a smooth line that climbs or falls as it overtakes, or is overtaken by, the others, and a circle at every period displays its rank. The Financial Times, The Economist and FiveThirtyEight use this format for league tables, polls and country rankings: it is the right choice when the order matters more than the exact values.

The data must be in long format, with one row per entity and period. By default `bump_chart()` computes the ranks for each period from the numeric `y` column (rank 1 = highest value, use `rankOrder = "asc"` to reverse). If your `y` column already holds ranks, set `ranked = TRUE`. Hover over a line to make it stand out.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
league <- data.frame(
  season = rep(c("2021", "2022", "2023", "2024"), each = 5),
  team   = rep(c("Lions", "Tigers", "Bears", "Wolves", "Eagles"), 4),
  points = c(80, 75, 60, 55, 50,
             70, 82, 58, 66, 49,
             65, 78, 72, 69, 52,
             60, 74, 81, 70, 77)
)

bump_chart(
  data  = league,
  x     = "season",
  y     = "points",
  group = "team",
  title = "League ranking by season"
)
```

Use `highlight` to bring a few entities forward and grey out the rest. Here are the GDP per capita ranks of eight Asian economies from the `gapminder` dataset:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gapminder)

countries <- c("Japan", "Singapore", "Hong Kong, China", "Taiwan",
               "Korea, Rep.", "Malaysia", "Thailand", "China")

gdp <- gapminder[gapminder$country %in% countries & gapminder$year >= 1967, ]
gdp$country <- as.character(gdp$country)

bump_chart(
  data      = gdp,
  x         = "year",
  y         = "gdpPercap",
  group     = "country",
  highlight = c("Singapore", "Korea, Rep."),
  title     = "GDP per capita rank, 1967-2007"
)
```

# `ridgeline_plot()`

A ridgeline plot, also known as a "joy plot", stacks several partially overlapping density curves, one per group, on a shared x-axis. The nickname comes from the cover of Joy Division's 1979 album *Unknown Pleasures*, which reproduces a 1970 plot of successive radio pulses from the first discovered pulsar. Claus Wilke's `ggridges` package made the format popular, and FiveThirtyEight and The Washington Post use it often. It is a good way to compare the shape of many distributions at once (shifts, spread, bimodality) without the space a grid of histograms would need.

The densities are computed in the browser with a Gaussian (default) or Epanechnikov kernel. By default, one joint bandwidth is picked from the pooled data with Silverman's rule of thumb, so every ridge is smoothed the same way. Lower ridges are drawn in front of the ones above them. Hovering a ridge or its label brings it to the front and shows its number of observations and mean.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2024)

reaction <- data.frame(
  time = c(rnorm(200, 300, 40), rnorm(200, 340, 50),
           rnorm(200, 380, 35), c(rnorm(100, 360, 25), rnorm(100, 460, 30)),
           rnorm(200, 420, 60)),
  condition = rep(c("Baseline", "Noise", "Fatigue", "Dual task", "Night"),
                  each = 200)
)

ridgeline_plot(
  data   = reaction,
  x      = "time",
  group  = "condition",
  sort   = "mean",
  stat   = "median",
  title  = "Reaction time by condition",
  xtitle = "Reaction time (ms)"
)
```

Use `overlap` to control how far each ridge reaches into the one above it, and `fill`, `fillOpacity` and `lineCol` to change the look. `fill` can be a single colour or a named vector with one colour per group:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset

ridgeline_plot(
  data        = mpg,
  x           = "hwy",
  group       = "class",
  sort        = "median",
  fill        = "#2c7fb8",
  lineCol     = "white",
  fillOpacity = 0.9,
  overlap     = 2,
  title       = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",
  xtitle      = "Highway miles per gallon"
)
```

# `treemap_chart()`

A treemap shows part-to-whole data as nested rectangles whose areas are proportional to a value. Ben Shneiderman invented the technique in the early 1990s. It became famous through SmartMoney's "Map of the Market" and the New York Times' graphics of the US federal budget. Use it when you have many parts (optionally grouped into categories) and want to see at a glance which ones dominate the total. When you supply a `group` column, tiles are coloured by group and each group gets a header showing its total. Hover over a tile to see its value and its share of the total.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
budget <- data.frame(
  department = c("Hospitals", "Primary care", "Public health",
                 "Schools", "Universities", "Vocational training",
                 "Army", "Navy", "Air force",
                 "Roads", "Railways", "Airports",
                 "Pensions", "Unemployment", "Family benefits"),
  ministry   = c("Health", "Health", "Health",
                 "Education", "Education", "Education",
                 "Defence", "Defence", "Defence",
                 "Transport", "Transport", "Transport",
                 "Social security", "Social security", "Social security"),
  spending   = c(5200, 2100, 800,
                 3900, 1800, 600,
                 2300, 1400, 1700,
                 1500, 1100, 400,
                 7400, 1900, 1300)
)

treemap_chart(
  data        = budget,
  value       = "spending",
  label       = "department",
  group       = "ministry",
  valueFormat = "$,.0f",
  title       = "Where the money goes (millions)"
)
```

Labels are truncated or hidden automatically when a tile is too small to fit them, so the chart stays readable even with many rectangles. In the example below, most of the 142 countries are too small to label, but you can hover over any tile to identify it.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

treemap_chart(
  data        = pop_2007,
  value       = "pop",
  label       = "country",
  group       = "continent",
  valueFormat = ".3~s",
  padding     = 1,
  title       = "World population in 2007"
)
```

# `waffle_chart()`

A waffle chart is a grid of squares, 10 x 10 by default, where each category fills a number of cells in proportion to its share of the whole. With 100 cells, each square reads as one percent, so "about a third" or "fewer than one in ten" is visible at a glance. Readers find this easier to judge than pie slices. Pew Research Center, FiveThirtyEight, The Economist and the Washington Post use the format often, and in R it was popularised by Bob Rudis's `waffle` package. Use it when a handful of categories make up a single whole, such as survey responses, vote shares or budget splits. Cells are allocated with the largest-remainder method, so the counts always add up exactly to the number of cells. Hover over a cell or a legend entry to highlight that category.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
survey <- data.frame(
  response = c("Strongly agree", "Agree", "Neutral",
               "Disagree", "Strongly disagree"),
  n = c(312, 405, 158, 87, 38)
)

waffle_chart(
  data     = survey,
  category = "response",
  value    = "n",
  colors   = c("#1a9641", "#a6d96a", "#bdbdbd", "#fdae61", "#d7191c"),
  title    = "Do you support the new policy?"
)
```

You can change the grid size with `rows` and `cols`, and the fill order with `direction = "col"`. The example below shows each continent's share of the world population in 2007 on a 10 x 20 grid, where each cell is half a percent:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]
pop_continent <- aggregate(pop ~ continent, data = pop_2007, FUN = sum)

waffle_chart(
  data      = pop_continent,
  category  = "continent",
  value     = "pop",
  direction = "col",
  rows      = 10,
  cols      = 20,
  title     = "World population by continent, 2007"
)
```

# `sunburst_chart()`

`sunburst_chart()` draws hierarchical data as concentric rings. It is inspired by the signature sunburst chart of [Apache ECharts](https://echarts.apache.org/) and reimplemented in plain D3. Hover over a sector to highlight its branch, click it to zoom in, and click the centre to zoom back out.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gapminder)

pop_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

sunburst_chart(
  data        = pop_2007,
  levels      = c("continent", "country"),
  value       = "pop",
  valueFormat = ".3~s",
  rootLabel   = "World",
  title       = "World population in 2007"
)
```

Without a `value` column, sectors are sized by row counts:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sunburst_chart(
  data        = mpg,
  levels      = c("class", "manufacturer"),
  rootLabel   = "Cars",
  labelRotate = "tangential",
  title       = "Number of car models by class and manufacturer"
)
```

# `radar_chart()`

`radar_chart()` draws one translucent polygon per series over a polygonal grid, with one spoke per variable. Its look and feel is inspired by the radar chart of [Chart.js](https://www.chartjs.org/). Polygons grow out from the center, hovering over a point shows its value, and clicking a legend entry toggles that series.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
players <- data.frame(
  player    = c("Ana", "Ben", "Chloe"),
  speed     = c(88, 72, 65),
  power     = c(60, 91, 70),
  passing   = c(79, 58, 93),
  dribbling = c(92, 64, 81),
  defending = c(45, 83, 74),
  stamina   = c(70, 77, 88)
)

radar_chart(
  data     = players,
  group    = "player",
  axes     = c("speed", "power", "passing", "dribbling", "defending", "stamina"),
  maxValue = 100,
  title    = "Player skill ratings"
)
```

When the variables are measured in different units, `scaleEachAxis = TRUE` gives each axis its own scale:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
cyl_means <- aggregate(cbind(mpg, hp, wt, qsec, disp) ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)
cyl_means$cyl <- paste(cyl_means$cyl, "cylinders")

radar_chart(
  data          = cyl_means,
  group         = "cyl",
  axisLabels    = c("Miles/gallon", "Horsepower", "Weight (1000 lbs)",
                    "1/4 mile time (s)", "Displacement (cu.in.)"),
  scaleEachAxis = TRUE,
  levels        = 4,
  gridShape     = "circle",
  valueFormat   = ".1f",
  title         = "mtcars averages by number of cylinders"
)
```

# `calendar_heatmap()`

`calendar_heatmap()` is inspired by the signature heatmap of [Frappe Charts](https://frappe.io/charts) and by GitHub's contribution graph. It draws one rounded square per day on a week-by-weekday grid, one panel per year, with a "Less ... More" legend and a staggered fade-in. Hover over a day to see its value, or over a legend square to highlight every day in that color bucket.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2024)
days <- seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day")
weekday <- !(format(days, "%u") %in% c("6", "7"))
activity <- data.frame(
  day     = days,
  commits = rpois(length(days), ifelse(weekday, 6, 1.5)) * rbinom(length(days), 1, 0.8)
)

calendar_heatmap(activity, date = "day", value = "commits", title = "Commits in 2024")
```

Data spanning several years is drawn as one panel per year:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
days <- seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "day")
season <- 10 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * as.numeric(format(days, "%j")) / 365)
rainfall <- data.frame(day = days, rain = pmax(0, rnorm(length(days), season, 6)))

calendar_heatmap(
  rainfall, date = "day", value = "rain", weekStart = "monday",
  colors = c("#9be9a8", "#40c463", "#30a14e", "#216e39"),
  valueLabel = "mm of rain", valueFormat = ",.1f",
  title = "Daily rainfall, 2021-2023"
)
```

# `chord_diagram()`

`chord_diagram()` shows the flows between a set of entities as outer arcs joined by ribbons. Its look and hover behaviour are inspired by the chord chart of [Nivo](https://nivo.rocks/chord/): hovering over an entity fades every ribbon not connected to it, and clicking an arc pins the highlight.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
migration <- data.frame(
  from  = c("Africa", "Africa", "Africa", "Asia", "Asia", "Asia",
            "Europe", "Europe", "Latin America", "Latin America",
            "North America", "Oceania", "Asia", "Europe"),
  to    = c("Europe", "North America", "Asia", "Europe", "North America",
            "Oceania", "North America", "Asia", "North America", "Europe",
            "Europe", "Asia", "Africa", "Oceania"),
  value = c(420, 150, 90, 610, 520, 230, 180, 120, 870, 260,
            95, 40, 60, 75)
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = migration,
  from        = "from",
  to          = "to",
  value       = "value",
  valueFormat = ",.0f",
  title       = "Migration flows between regions (illustrative data)"
)
```

A square matrix with dimnames works too:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
hair <- matrix(
  c(11975,  5871, 8916, 2868,
     1951, 10048, 2060, 6171,
     8010, 16145, 8090, 8045,
     1013,   990,  940, 6907),
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"),
                  c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"))
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = hair,
  colors      = c("#3b3b3b", "#f2c45a", "#8c5a3c", "#d0533a"),
  ribbonColor = "gradient",
  padAngle    = 0.05,
  valueFormat = ",.0f",
  title       = "Hair color flows"
)
```

# `streamgraph()`

`streamgraph()` is inspired by the [Highcharts](https://www.highcharts.com/) streamgraph: stacked areas flowing around a centred (wiggle) baseline, with labels drawn inside each layer, a crosshair tooltip and an interactive legend. Unlike `stacked_area_chart()`, it takes long data. Hover over a layer to highlight it, and click a legend item to hide or show it.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2024)
years  <- 1980:2020
genres <- c("Rock", "Pop", "Hip hop", "Electronic", "Country",
            "R&B", "Jazz", "Metal", "Reggae", "Latin")
peaks  <- c(1984, 1999, 2012, 2008, 1993, 2003, 1981, 1990, 1986, 2018)
sizes  <- c(60, 55, 70, 40, 30, 35, 18, 25, 15, 45)
music  <- expand.grid(year = years, genre = genres)
idx    <- match(music$genre, genres)
music$listeners <- round(
  sizes[idx] * exp(-((music$year - peaks[idx]) / 9)^2) + runif(nrow(music), 1, 6)
)

streamgraph(
  data        = music,
  x           = "year",
  group       = "genre",
  value       = "listeners",
  valueFormat = ",.0f",
  xtitle      = "Year",
  title       = "Music genres, 1980-2020 (simulated listeners)"
)
```

`offset = "expand"` turns the stream into a 100% stacked view:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
phones <- data.frame(
  year   = rep(as.numeric(rownames(WorldPhones)), ncol(WorldPhones)),
  region = factor(rep(colnames(WorldPhones), each = nrow(WorldPhones)),
                  levels = colnames(WorldPhones)),
  phones = as.vector(WorldPhones)
)

streamgraph(phones, x = "year", group = "region", value = "phones",
            offset = "expand", order = "descending", curve = "monotoneX",
            colorPalette = "Set2", title = "Share of telephones by region")
```

# `violin_plot()`

`violin_plot()` reproduces the look of [Plotly.js](https://plotly.com/javascript/) violin traces. Each group gets a mirrored kernel density, with an optional inner box plot, jittered raw points, and a hover tooltip showing the summary statistics.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
violin_plot(
  data   = iris,
  y      = "Sepal.Length",
  group  = "Species",
  title  = "Sepal length by species",
  ytitle = "Sepal length (cm)"
)
```

Use `points = "all"` to show every observation, `meanline` to mark the mean, `sort` to order the violins, and `scale = "count"` to make each violin's width proportional to its group size:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
violin_plot(
  data         = mpg,
  y            = "hwy",
  group        = "class",
  points       = "all",
  meanline     = TRUE,
  sort         = "median",
  colorPalette = "Tableau10",
  title        = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",
  ytitle       = "Highway miles per gallon"
)
```

# `mosaic_chart()`

`mosaic_chart()` draws a mosaic (Marimekko) chart, inspired by the mosaic example in the [Vega-Lite](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/) gallery. Each column's width is that category's share of the total, and each column is split into segments that add up to 100%, so every cell's area is proportional to its count. Hover over a cell to see its count, its column's share and its share within the column.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
titanic <- as.data.frame(Titanic)

mosaic_chart(
  data   = titanic,
  x      = "Class",
  fill   = "Survived",
  value  = "Freq",
  colors = c("#e45756", "#4c78a8"),
  xtitle = "Share of passengers and crew",
  ytitle = "Share within class",
  title  = "Who survived the Titanic?"
)
```

When `value` is omitted, rows are counted. Factor levels set the order of the columns and segments:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
cars <- mtcars
cars$cyl  <- factor(cars$cyl,  levels = c(8, 6, 4), labels = c("8 cyl", "6 cyl", "4 cyl"))
cars$gear <- factor(cars$gear, levels = c(3, 4, 5), labels = c("3 gears", "4 gears", "5 gears"))

mosaic_chart(cars, x = "cyl", fill = "gear", labelType = "both",
             legendTitle = "Gears", title = "Motor Trend cars: gears by cylinders")
```

# `radial_bar_chart()`

`radial_bar_chart()` draws each category as a concentric circular progress track, inspired by the radialBar chart of [ApexCharts](https://apexcharts.com/). Each ring has a faint background track and a rounded arc that sweeps in on load, a label sits at the start of each track, and the average (or total) is shown in the center. Hover over a ring to put its name and value in the center.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
platforms <- data.frame(
  platform = c("Vimeo", "Messenger", "Facebook", "LinkedIn"),
  share    = c(76, 67, 61, 90)
)

radial_bar_chart(
  data  = platforms,
  label = "platform",
  value = "share",
  title = "Weekly active users (share of total, illustrative)"
)
```

With `max` you can set the value that fills a whole ring, and with `endAngle = 360` the tracks make a full circle:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sales <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"),
  units  = c(420, 310, 275, 190, 120)
)

radial_bar_chart(
  data        = sales,
  label       = "region",
  value       = "units",
  max         = 500,
  endAngle    = 360,
  centerValue = "total",
  centerLabel = "Units sold",
  title       = "Units sold by region (target: 500)"
)
```

# `rose_chart()`

`rose_chart()` draws a Nightingale rose, also called a coxcomb or polar area chart. It is inspired by the polar-interval rose chart of [AntV G2](https://g2.antv.antgroup.com/). Every category gets a wedge of the same angle, and the radius follows a square-root scale so that each wedge's area stays proportional to its value. An optional `group` column stacks the wedges. The example below uses Florence Nightingale's own monthly death counts from the Crimean War, 1854–55 (the same values as `HistData::Nightingale`).

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
mon <- c("Apr 1854", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov",
         "Dec", "Jan 1855", "Feb", "Mar")
crimea <- data.frame(
  month  = factor(rep(mon, times = 3), levels = mon),
  cause  = factor(rep(c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes"), each = 12),
                  levels = c("Preventable disease", "Wounds", "Other causes")),
  deaths = c(1, 12, 11, 359, 828, 788, 503, 844, 1725, 2761, 2120, 1205,
             0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 81, 132, 287, 114, 83, 42, 32,
             5, 9, 6, 23, 30, 70, 128, 106, 131, 324, 361, 172)
)

rose_chart(
  data     = crimea,
  category = "month",
  value    = "deaths",
  group    = "cause",
  colors   = c("#7fa7c9", "#e0645c", "#4d4d4d"),
  title    = "Causes of death in the army in the East, 1854-55",
  height   = 560
)
```

Use `sort` to order the wedges by size:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rose_chart(
  data        = data.frame(state = rownames(USArrests)[1:12],
                           murder = USArrests$Murder[1:12]),
  category    = "state",
  value       = "murder",
  sort        = "desc",
  valueFormat = ".1f",
  title       = "Murder arrests per 100,000 residents (1973)"
)
```

# `hexbin_plot()`

`hexbin_plot()` is inspired by the hexbin transform of [Observable Plot](https://observablehq.com/plot/transforms/hexbin). It groups points into a grid of hexagons coloured by the number of observations in each one, which keeps dense scatter plots readable. The binning is written by hand, since d3-hexbin is not bundled with r2d3.

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
hexbin_plot(
  data     = faithful,
  x        = "waiting",
  y        = "eruptions",
  binWidth = 14,
  xtitle   = "Waiting time to next eruption (min)",
  ytitle   = "Eruption duration (min)",
  title    = "Old Faithful eruptions"
)
```

A log colour scale helps when counts are very skewed:

```{r fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
dsample <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 10000), ]

hexbin_plot(
  data         = dsample,
  x            = "carat",
  y            = "price",
  binWidth     = 8,
  colorPalette = "Viridis",
  colorScale   = "log",
  title        = "Diamond price by carat"
)
```

# Using `ddplot` in `Shiny`

Every `ddplot` chart is an `r2d3` htmlwidget, so in a `Shiny` app you can use `r2d3::d3Output()` in the UI and `r2d3::renderD3()` in the server. When an input changes, the chart is redrawn in place with the new data and options:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(ddplot)
library(r2d3)

ui <- fluidPage(

  h2("Example ddplot application"),

  selectInput(
    inputId = "colors",
    label = "Point color",
    choices = colors(),
    selected = "springgreen3"
  ),

  sliderInput(
    inputId = "slider",
    label = "Point size",
    min = 1,
    max = 10,
    value = 3
  ),

  d3Output("scatter", height = "450px")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$scatter <- renderD3({
    scatter_plot(
      data = iris,
      x = "Sepal.Length",
      y = "Sepal.Width",
      size = input$slider,
      col = input$colors
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```
